paragraphs.text: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair is characterized by facial features that resemble but are not completely typical of Noonan syndrome, together with a behavioral phenotype, growth hormone (GH) deficiency, and a distinctive combination of ectodermal abnormalities, including darkly pigmented, hairless skin and loose anagen hair (Mazzanti et al., 2003). Affected individuals show reduced growth, often associated with proven GH deficiency, cognitive deficits, distinctive hyperactive behavior, hypernasal voice, cardiac anomalies, and easily pluckable, sparse, thin, slow-growing hair (Cordeddu et al., 2009).

paragraphs.text: Tosti et al. (1997) reviewed 19 patients diagnosed with loose anagen hair (14 children and 5 adults). Associated conditions included Noonan syndrome in a 5-year-old boy. In all cases, the trichogram showed a predominance of anagen hairs (80 to 100%) devoid of sheaths. The authors concluded that loose anagen hair may be sporadic, may occur together with developmental or acquired conditions, or, less commonly, may be familial.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) described 25 unrelated, sporadic subjects with the SHOC2 S2G mutation. They exhibited reduced growth, which was frequently associated with proven GH deficiency, cognitive deficits, distinctive hyperactive behavior that improved with age in most subjects, hypernasal voice, and hair anomalies including easily pluckable, sparse, thin, slow-growing hair; loose anagen hair was confirmed microscopically in 12. Some had darkly pigmented skin, eczema, or ichthyosis. Cardiac anomalies included mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects, which were overrepresented compared with the general Noonan syndrome population. Other features in some subjects included macrocephaly, high forehead, hypertelorism, palpebral ptosis, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, short webbed neck, and pectus anomalies. Referring pediatricians felt that several subjects had features suggestive of Costello or cardiofaciocutaneous (CFC) syndrome as newborns or young infants.

paragraphs.text: Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) reported 8 patients with the SHOC2 S2G mutation. All showed short stature, sparse hair, and atopic skin. Six showed severe mental retardation and easily pluckable hair, and 1 showed leukocytosis. paragraphs.text: Hoban et al. (2012) reported a male infant with a de novo SHOC2 S2G mutation who presented with fetal distress requiring premature delivery at 32 weeks. After birth he was noted to have dysmorphic features, edema, hepatosplenomegaly, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and respiratory distress. Echocardiography revealed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction, which progressed rapidly, leading to discharge for palliative care. The authors noted that his cardiac findings and other features were not typical of patients previously reported with this mutation and concluded that the case expanded the clinical phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Gripp et al. (2013) reported 5 males with the SHOC2 S2G mutation, 4 of whom had initially been suspected of having Costello syndrome. All had skin hyperpigmentation, sparse light-colored hair, increased fine wrinkles, ligamentous laxity, and developmental delay, and all 4 with available data had a structural cardiac anomaly. The light-colored, slow-growing scalp hair with dolichocilia resembled the hair seen in Costello syndrome caused by HRAS G13C. Brain imaging showed relative megalencephaly, enlarged subarachnoid spaces suggestive of benign external hydrocephalus, and a small posterior fossa with a vertical tentorium. Including previously reported patients, Chiari 1 malformation was present in 3 of 8 SHOC2 mutation-positive patients with MRI data; the authors attributed it to the combination of relative megalencephaly with a small posterior fossa and noted that it can develop after birth.

paragraphs.text: Patient 1 of Gripp et al. (2013) was born after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios and cystic hygroma and had macrosomia, pyloric stenosis, severe failure to thrive requiring a gastrostomy tube, mild pulmonic valve stenosis, low axial tone, small optic nerves, delayed motor development, macrocephaly (OFC +3 SD) with a large anterior fontanel, sparse thin hair, ptosis, hepatosplenomegaly, hemangiomata, and fine wrinkling of the hands. Brain imaging showed enlarged subarachnoid spaces, a vertical tentorium with small posterior fossa, mild cerebellar tonsillar ectopia, and a thin corpus callosum. He developed primary myelofibrosis, with blasts in peripheral blood and a markedly hypercellular marrow with increased reticulin staining, and died at age 2.5 years after splenectomy in preparation for a bone marrow transplant. Patient 2, born to a 21-year-old mother and a 40-year-old father after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios, had increased birth weight, macrocephaly, ptosis, posteriorly angulated ears, increased palmar wrinkling, loose skin, bilateral inguinal hernias, and hypotonia, prompting consideration of Costello syndrome. He had severe feeding difficulties, a subdural effusion requiring drainage, delayed bone age, and nonverbal intellectual disability; at age 9 5/12 years his height was at the 3rd to 5th centile, and he had acanthosis nigricans, eczema, and dry skin. Brain MRI showed ventriculomegaly, hypogenesis of the corpus callosum, decreased white matter volume, an abnormally vertical tentorium, and cerebellar tonsillar ectopia.

paragraphs.text: Patient 3 of Gripp et al. (2013) was born after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios and had macrosomia, tracheostenosis, chronic lung disease, and a neonatal seizure. He had right bundle branch block and mild to moderate biventricular hypertrophic cardiomyopathy at age 6 months, as well as aortic insufficiency and mild pulmonic stenosis. He required a gastrostomy for failure to thrive. He had developmental delay and aggressive behavior and was diagnosed with pervasive developmental disorder and Tourette syndrome at 9 years. At age 9 years his height was 125 cm (10th centile), weight 29.4 kg (50th centile), and OFC 60 cm (+5 SD). Other features included coarse facial features, mild ptosis, eczema, a cafe-au-lait lesion, deep palmar creases, osteoporosis, and strabismus; brain imaging showed enlarged arachnoid spaces and decreased white matter volume. Patient 4, of Mexican ancestry, was born at 37 weeks' gestation weighing 2.9 kg to a 32-year-old mother and a 41-year-old father. He had failure to thrive, elevated PT/PTT, rectal prolapse, strabismus, nystagmus, chronic ear infections, atrial septal defect, trivial mitral regurgitation, severe eczema, sparse, thin, easily pluckable blond hair, long eyelashes, mild to moderate intellectual disability, short stature, webbed neck, pectus excavatum, and widely spaced nipples, but no macrocephaly. Brain MRI showed mild ventriculomegaly and periventricular nodular heterotopia; MRIs at 6 years, performed because of headaches, revealed development of a Chiari 1 malformation in the context of platybasia and basilar invagination, and fusion of the C3 and C4 vertebrae. Patient 5 had neonatal hypotonia and feeding difficulties requiring a nasogastric tube until about age 1 year. A brain MRI at 3 weeks showed a relatively small cerebellar vermis and hemispheres with prominent fluid spaces and increased extra-axial fluid spaces. He had a patent ductus arteriosus, an abnormal mitral valve with 3 papillary muscles, a duplicated renal collecting system, short stature, macrocephaly (OFC +2 SD), hemangiomata, dry hyperpigmented skin, slow-growing hair that was not easily pluckable, fine motor delay, and attention deficit disorder; he was last reported at 8 3/12 years.

checks.claim: Motta et al. (2019) identified a c.807_808delinsTT mutation in the SHOC2 gene, resulting in a gln269_his270delinsHisTyr substitution, in a patient with a RASopathy.
checks.evidence_quote: Here, we report on the third RASopathy-causing SHOC2 mutation (c.807_808delinsTT, p.Gln269_His270delinsHisTyr)
checks.explanation: The variant notation matches the abstract.

checks.claim: The SHOC2 Q269_H270delinsHY mutant protein showed enhanced binding to MRAS and PPP1CB.
checks.evidence_quote: revealing enhanced binding of the mutant protein to MRAS and PPP1CB

checks.claim: The SHOC2 Q269_H270delinsHY mutant protein increased MAPK signaling.
checks.evidence_quote: and increased signaling through the MAPK cascade

checks.claim: Unlike SHOC2 S2G, the SHOC2 Q269_H270delinsHY mutant protein was not constitutively targeted to the plasma membrane.
checks.evidence_quote: Differing from SHOC2 S2G , SHOC2 Q269_H270delinsHY is not constitutively targeted to the plasma membrane.
